questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A trauma patient has pulsatile extremity bleeding that continues despite firm direct pressure. What is the priority action?
choices: Remove the dressing repeatedly to inspect the wound
Apply an approved tourniquet according to training, tighten until bleeding stops, and document the time
Elevate the limb and wait for a hemoglobin result
Loosen pressure every five minutes
questions.explanation: Life-threatening extremity hemorrhage requires prompt tourniquet use when direct pressure fails. The device is secured, timed, kept visible, and not periodically loosened while major bleeding continues.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which finding may be an early clue to hemorrhagic shock even when systolic pressure remains normal?
choices: Warm dry skin with stable mentation
Restlessness, cool skin, tachypnea, tachycardia, and narrowing pulse pressure
A healed abrasion
One near-baseline hemoglobin result
questions.explanation: Compensation can preserve systolic pressure early. Subtle mentation change, cool skin, tachypnea, tachycardia and narrowing pulse pressure can precede hypotension; initial hemoglobin can also lag blood loss.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: An unstable trauma patient has severe respiratory distress, unilateral absent breath sounds, and hypotension. What is the priority concern?
choices: Tension pneumothorax requiring immediate trauma intervention
A minor rib contusion
Chronic anemia
Anxiety only
questions.explanation: This cue cluster suggests tension physiology and obstructive shock. In an unstable patient, immediate protocol-directed decompression should not be delayed for routine imaging.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Where should a pelvic binder be positioned for suspected unstable pelvic-ring injury with shock?
choices: Around the waist above the iliac crests
At the level of the greater trochanters
Across the lower ribs
Directly over the knees
questions.explanation: A binder stabilizes the pelvic ring when centered over the greater trochanters. Waist-level placement is too high; repeated pelvic springing should be avoided because it can disrupt clot formation.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A FAST examination is negative, but a trauma patient remains pale, confused, tachycardic, and hypotensive with pelvic injury. Which interpretation is safest?
choices: The negative FAST excludes internal hemorrhage
FAST can miss pelvic, retroperitoneal or early bleeding, so hemorrhage evaluation and control must continue
The shock must be psychological
CT is always required before any intervention
questions.explanation: FAST answers limited questions and does not exclude all bleeding compartments. Persistent shock requires continued search and rapid trauma source control rather than false reassurance.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which plan best reflects damage-control resuscitation for major traumatic hemorrhage?
choices: Large unmonitored crystalloid volumes until pressure is normal
Early MTP activation, warmed whole blood or balanced components, limited unnecessary crystalloid, and rapid hemorrhage control
Red blood cells only with no coagulation assessment
Vasopressors instead of blood and surgery
questions.explanation: Damage-control resuscitation integrates hemostatic blood replacement, warming, correction of coagulopathy and calcium abnormalities, and definitive control while avoiding excessive crystalloid dilution.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which abnormalities form the trauma 'lethal diamond' that can amplify bleeding?
choices: Hypertension, alkalosis, hyperthermia, and hypercalcemia
Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypocalcemia
Fever, hypernatremia, bradycardia, and leukocytosis
Pain, nausea, insomnia, and constipation
questions.explanation: Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy and hypocalcemia reinforce hemorrhage and cardiovascular dysfunction. Active warming, blood-based resuscitation and laboratory-guided correction address this cycle.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which finding most strongly suggests that a trauma patient is only a transient responder to resuscitation?
choices: Perfusion and vital signs remain stable after definitive hemostasis
Pressure briefly improves after blood and then falls again with worsening tachycardia
The patient reports less pain after analgesia
Temperature rises toward normal with warming
questions.explanation: Temporary improvement followed by recurrent shock suggests ongoing hemorrhage. More resuscitation may be needed, but definitive operative, procedural or endovascular control remains the priority.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which statement about tranexamic acid in trauma is accurate?
choices: It is routinely given to every injured patient
It may benefit selected significantly bleeding patients when given early, generally within three hours, under protocol
It replaces hemorrhage control
It reverses every anticoagulant
questions.explanation: TXA is a time-sensitive adjunct for selected hemorrhage risk and should follow the local protocol. It neither replaces blood and source control nor serves as a universal anticoagulant reversal agent.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: After an intervention during trauma resuscitation, what is the most important nursing action?
choices: Continue to the secondary survey without interruption
Repeat XABCDE and compare airway, breathing, bleeding, perfusion, neurologic status, and temperature
Wait for all laboratory results before reassessment
Document only the final blood pressure
questions.explanation: Trauma status changes rapidly. Repeating the primary survey after every intervention and deterioration reveals treatment response and new life threats before moving to lower-priority assessment.
